en: Subdued the hell of the cutting wind,
Akjoltoy held it down,
And opened up the day,
Making it brilliantly bright.
Great Bilgich’s fury left him,
And he came out into the sunlight.
That Bilgich ceased his infernal raging
And regained his speech.
When he rode out from the Great Khagan,
Great Bilgich fixed his hatred
On Akjoltoy and the valiant Seytek.
Intent on taking Kulunsur as spoil,
He charged with a roar,
Leveling his spear with a battle cry.
As he was about to reach Akjoltoy,
Brave Seytek, that peerless lion, thought:
“If the infidel reaches my uncle,
Then afterward, upon this land,
The end of days will surely fall.
I shall drive my horse without restraint
And bar the path
Of this wrathful calamity.”
So saying, brave Seytek
Turned all his attention there;
He loomed like Mount Opol,
While Kulunsur beneath him
Wheeled as he gripped his spear.
He reined the cloud-swift steed
Hard against the fetlocks,
And that matchless Kulunsur
Turned his neck toward the foe.
With a stout shaft and keen point,
The tasselled Syr spear—
“Creator, grant me passage!” he cried,
And straight at great Bilgich
He thrust it with a thunderous roar.
His eyes blazed like a lion’s;
His broad white teeth seemed set like stakes,
Teeth worthy of royal blood,
And he ground them section by section.
He roused a terrible rage,
Counting his precious life as a hair,
And launched a furious assault,
Hurling the spear with all his strength.
At the bristling boar
Before he could truly reach Joltoy,
He aimed for the face of the elbow,
The very brink of waiting death,
Between the lungs and heart,
The measured mark of mortal doom,
Level with the ribs:
“If I strike him exactly here, I have him!”
He chose the mortal spot,
Lashed Kulunsur with the whip,
And before that hulking champion
Could reach the hero Joltoy,
The peerless warrior struck Bilgich
With his spear.
His senses failed and his strength ebbed;
At that moment great Bilgich
Reeled unconscious and bewildered.
What could poor Bilgich do?
Unable to achieve his aim,
Though Akjoltoy was his chosen target,
He could not kill him and ride away;
Seytek struck him with the spear,
And when Seytek’s spear struck,
He fell backward from the saddle,
His feet slipped from the stirrups,
And both his legs dangled loose.
As though something now seized his skirts,
His two eyes rolled wildly.
His surging courage vanished,
His frenzy crumbled and was quelled;
He had collided with brave Seytek
And made ready to flee.
That roaring boar—
Where now had all his fury gone?
When champion meets champion,
Both men’s legs begin to twitch;
When one tongue answers another,
The hinges of their jaws begin to quiver.
Bilgich’s spirit nearly left him;
The falsehood of this accursed world
Was laid bare before him.
Bilgich despaired of life,
All strength deserted the warrior,
Blood poured from his side,
And grievous was his wound.
Unable to gain his desire,
His reins cut through together,
He had collided with a leopard of a hero,
Encountered a man of majesty,
And fallen upon a wrathful foe.
His horse was swift and huge,
The winged gray Kerik;
No wind could match him at a trot,
No beast could match him at a walk.
A message had been tied to his tail:
“He will catch whatever man he pursues”—
And so they named him Gray Kerik.
Gray Kerik, bred for battle,
Could halt atop a mountain;
For nine full years they had watched him,
Letting him graze untouched by tether.
They had raised him in darkness,
And Niyanker, whose eye was keen,
Had approved him as a master judge of horses.
Carrying Bilgich off,
He sped toward the Khagan.
Over ridge after ridge,
Through gaping valley lands,
Skirting Imerchik,
Across Kürküldök’s gray plain,
And farther down the road he roamed,
Fleeing all alone.
Seytek was a reckless, simple-hearted hero;
He knew nothing of this,
Nor did brave Seytek know
How many perils lay in Beijing.
There were countless excavated pits
And misery for any who encountered them;
That scorched boar
Had troops stationed in the trenches,
His venom lay in many places,
His infernal wrath was stored in ambush,
And the overthrown Bilgich
Still possessed all his cunning.
There were sentries and boundaries,
And warriors stationed at every frontier;
Words would fail if all were told—
That accursed one had many stratagems,
Every kind of calamity was there.
Knowing nothing of those dangers,
With skirts loose and breast exposed,
The gray-maned hero Seytek
Still bore the fault of innocence.
He pursued the cunning fugitive:
Black without and cold within,
He chased the sorcerer, saying,
“If I do not turn Kulunsur’s head,
If I do not pursue this maddened Bilgich
All the way to Beijing itself!”
“If I do not shatter his throne and game,
If I do not slaughter this hulking slave,
If I do not hew clean through his neck,
If I do not catch, devour, and butcher him,
May I sink into darkness as though never born!
They used to say that the foe who flees
Will take for his wife
The finest of black-haired beauties,
The best among all women.
But I shall spill his blood at last;
I shall seize him by the trailing hem,
And cast that accursed, doomed Bilgich
To be torn apart in the gray-wolf game.
The people will clamor in uproar,
And despair of their wrathful champion;
They will say, ‘He was born of a noble man,’
And my lineage will become known.
All forty khanates of China
Will understand and despair of life!”
So spoke brave Seytek,
Consumed by fierce intent,
Brandishing and driving with his spear.
His eyes fixed on great Bilgich,
He followed directly behind,
While the black earth, though not split in two,
Endured the pounding through its depths.
Every rise was gouged away;
Wherever the hooves struck squarely,
Trenches were carved like canals.
It became tumult, calamity, and strife,
A terror no living soul could bear.
When they entered the downward slope,
Brave Bilgich’s great Kerik
Stretched his forelegs like a deer;
When they began climbing uphill,
Kulunsur swept on like a whirlwind—
Such was the ground of their pursuit.
Amid this tale of endless tumult,
They had now drawn close
To the place established as an ambush,
Where Bilgich’s army lay concealed.
Unable to bear his wounds,
Yet still the warrior Akjoltoy
Had ridden after Seytek.
Upon the matchless Kulunsur,
He whipped him right and left,
Spurred him on from either side,
And shouted in anger,
Calling out to Khan Seytek.
Kulunsur, whom no living creature could catch,
Shot whirring like an arrow;
When he passed over black stones,
They burst apart like charcoal.
Ah, wondrous beast Kulunsur,
He flew rumbling like a cloud,
His tail streaming over his haunches,
His matchless breeding plain to see.
From the black mountains of Kaspang,
From the mouth of Kapka-Tash,
From the heights of Dyngsha,
From the fortress no mortal had entered,
The stronghold firmly sealed,
Uncle Joltoy caught up
At the ridge of the Sentry Stone.
He tugged at his armor,
Shaking him about the head and eyes:
“You have courage but no sense;
You are a witless Seytek!
By refusing to heed advice,
Will you send Joltoy to the grave?
To a place where no man can pass,
Will you cast us upon the embers?
Without even binding our hands and feet,
Will you cast us into the fire?
Alas, Seytek, may ruin take you—
My child, what if the two of us are parted?
Did I not tell you before
That the accursed Khagan
Has paths narrower than a hair
And passes even I cannot cross?
“In Beijing, where wrath cannot penetrate,
His people swarm like black beetles.
This is the great nation of China,
A place where men settle only for battle,
Where your first forefather led the charge
And the land sucked dry all who fought.
There, parted from his lions,
Your first forefather met his end.
It is no cheap land like an open ridge,
Nor is Bilgich a common warrior.
If we go any farther,
There are iron-walled enclosures
And deeply excavated pits.
There are armies of that madman,
So dense the sun cannot be seen.
Anyone who falls in cannot leap back out;
Their stubborn traps are hell itself.
That senseless scourge
Commands a well-arrayed host of ten thousand.
Once locked in combat, they never retreat;
It is a radiant and exalted land,
Where the people of Chin-Machin dwell.
Their warriors butcher any who provoke them;
They are a people who ask, ‘Where is strife?’
Whenever one among them dies,
They roast and eat another.
When their giant rage possesses them,
They strike down and eat any crow they see,
And surround and devour any wild ass.
They flare up anew whenever diminished;
No living being has ever reached their root.
Though slaughter lasts for years,
Their baleful power never fades,
